name: AIRO
one_line: Wristband with a spectrometer meant to passively detect calories and nutrients from your bloodstream after eating.
audience: Quantified-self consumers who refused to log food manually
stated_cause: The company received market feedback that it "lacked the proof that a product like AIRO would work as advertised" and admitted it should have tested and validated the device further before putting it up for sale; it cancelled all pre-orders and issued full refunds.

name: Humane AI Pin
one_line: Screenless wearable AI assistant with a laser-projected display meant to replace the smartphone.
audience: Early-adopter consumers wanting a post-phone ambient assistant
stated_cause: Underwhelming sales and functionality criticism; daily returns eventually outnumbered sales, the price was cut from $699 to $499, and HP bought the assets for $116M after Humane had raised $230M — every shipped Pin was bricked on 2025-02-28.

name: Jibo
one_line: The first consumer social home robot — a swivelling desk companion with a face, voice and personality.
audience: Families wanting an emotional presence rather than a smart speaker
stated_cause: Ran out of money in 2018 after raising ~$73M; shipped at $899 while costing far more than an Echo and doing less, hit by delays, thin app integration and competition from Alexa and Google Assistant. Servers were shut off in March 2019 and the robots delivered a farewell message.

name: Kuri (Mayfield Robotics)
one_line: Bosch-backed home robot that roamed the house, filmed family moments and responded to people.
audience: Families with young children
stated_cause: "After extensive review, there was not a business fit within Bosch to support and scale our business" — production stopped July 2018 and all operations ceased 2018-10-31 as social home robots failed to justify their price against cheap voice assistants.

name: Moxie (Embodied)
one_line: $799 desktop robot that held conversations, taught social-emotional skills and acted as an emotional-support companion for children.
audience: Parents of children aged 5-10, marketed heavily to families of autistic kids
stated_cause: A critical funding round collapsed when the lead investor pulled out at the last minute and no replacement was found; because the LLM, speech recognition and emotional-inference layers all ran on Embodied's cloud, every robot was bricked and no refunds were offered.

name: Mycroft AI
one_line: Open-source, privacy-respecting voice assistant and the Mark II smart speaker, built as an Alexa/Google Home alternative.
audience: Privacy-focused consumers and open-source hobbyists
stated_cause: Ran out of money — the CEO said that without immediate new investment they would have to cease development; "the single most expensive item that could not be predicted was ongoing litigation against a non-practicing patent entity," and remaining Kickstarter rewards went unfulfilled.

name: Zeo
one_line: Bedside sleep coach with an EEG headband that staged your sleep and scored it nightly.
audience: Quantified-self early adopters with sleep problems
stated_cause: The founder cited a business model with "suboptimal profit margin", the invasiveness of the headband, and friction from having to log into a website to add data; at $400 it was too expensive and too complex for the market, and it was outpaced by Fitbit-class entrants. Raised $20.6M.

name: Google Glass (Explorer Edition)
one_line: Head-worn display with camera and voice control, sold to consumers as the next computing platform.
audience: General consumers and early adopters
stated_cause: Marketed as a finished consumer product while still in development, creating unrealistic expectations; criticised for high price, unclear value proposition and privacy concerns, and banned from venues. Google ended the Explorer programme and stopped consumer sales in January 2015.

name: Magic Leap One (consumer AR)
one_line: Spatial-computing AR headset launched with consumer ambitions at $2,300.
audience: Consumers and prosumers expecting mainstream AR
stated_cause: "Awkwardly straddled the consumer and enterprise segment" at an unsustainable price, forcing the company to lay off roughly half its workforce and abandon consumer ambitions to refocus on enterprise two years after launch; by 2026 it exited headsets entirely to become a waveguide supplier.

name: openmargin
one_line: Social e-reader letting readers share margin notes on the same book with each other.
audience: Book clubs, students and social readers
stated_cause: "Being too early in the market", compounded by slow shipping and strong competitors.

name: Vreal
one_line: Platform for streaming and watching VR gameplay from inside the virtual world.
audience: VR gamers and streaming audiences
stated_cause: Described as "ahead of their time in a market not fully developed" — the installed VR base never reached the size the streaming model required.

name: Tandem (live fitness streaming)
one_line: Live-streamed workout classes taught by fitness influencers.
audience: Home exercisers wanting live group classes
stated_cause: The founders concluded "live fitness isn't that engaging", and influencers were reluctant to adopt a new platform.

name: Tandem App (medication management)
one_line: App to help patients remember and manage their medication schedules.
audience: Patients on multi-drug regimens
stated_cause: After launching, the team discovered retention was really difficult despite initial research validating the need, and decided not to continue.

name: Amazon Halo
one_line: Screenless health band plus service scoring body composition, activity, sleep and even vocal tone of voice.
audience: Mainstream consumers wanting whole-body health insight
stated_cause: Amazon's VP of smart home and health told staff the Halo line was sunset due to "significant headwinds, including an increasingly crowded segment and uncertain economic conditions," as part of broader cost cutting; all devices stopped working 2023-08-01.

name: Amazon Glow
one_line: $300 projector-and-camera device for kids to play games and read books during video calls with distant relatives.
audience: Families separated by distance, especially travelling parents and grandparents
stated_cause: Discontinued after roughly a year due to poor sales and changing customer behaviour — it was a product designed for the pandemic era released as normal life resumed.

name: Spotify Car Thing
one_line: Dashboard touchscreen dedicated to controlling Spotify playback in the car.
audience: Drivers with older cars lacking CarPlay/Android Auto
stated_cause: Production ended in July 2022 citing low consumer interest and supply chain issues; Spotify then bricked all devices on 2024-12-09 "as part of our ongoing efforts to streamline our product offerings". The device lost Spotify $31.4 million.

name: Sora (OpenAI consumer app)
one_line: Social app for generating and sharing AI video, including cameos of real people.
audience: General consumers and creators making short AI video
stated_cause: Burned roughly $1 million per day in compute against an estimated $2.1 million in lifetime in-app purchase revenue; active users fell from ~1 million to under 500,000, Disney exited its $1B partnership, and OpenAI redirected resources to coding tools and ChatGPT.

name: Huxe
one_line: App that turned any prompt into a generated personal podcast or podcast series, built by ex-NotebookLM engineers.
audience: Commuters and knowledge workers wanting a daily audio briefing
stated_cause: No reason was specified, but the shutdown came one day after Spotify shipped a near-identical personal podcast feature; the startup's core product had become a commoditised feature at Adobe, Amazon, ElevenLabs, Meta and Spotify. Had raised $4.6M.

name: Dot (New Computer)
one_line: AI companion that grew more personalised over time and acted as a friend, confidante and source of emotional support.
audience: Individuals wanting a persistent AI relationship rather than a task assistant
stated_cause: "We came to the shared realization that our Northstars as founders had diverged. Rather than compromise either vision, we've decided to go our separate ways and wind down operations." Appfigures measured only 24,500 lifetime iOS downloads.

name: Artifact
one_line: AI-personalised news reader from Instagram's founders that later added social commenting.
audience: News-hungry consumers wanting an algorithmic feed without a social network
stated_cause: Kevin Systrom: "We have built something that a core group of users love, but we have concluded that the market opportunity isn't big enough to warrant continued investment in this way."

name: IRL
one_line: Group-messaging and events social app that raised over $200M at unicorn valuation.
audience: Gen Z organising group hangouts and events
stated_cause: An internal investigation found that 95% of IRL's users "weren't real — they were either automated or bots"; the board voted to shut down.

name: Poparazzi
one_line: Anti-selfie photo app where only your friends could post pictures of you.
audience: Gen Z friend groups
stated_cause: Hit #1 on the App Store in 2021 but could not convert the viral spike into sustained usage; the team wound the app down and gave users until 2023-06-30 to export content. Day-30 retention for this cohort of viral social apps sat under 5%.

name: Meerkat
one_line: Live mobile video streaming app that broadcast to your Twitter followers.
audience: Early live-streamers and their social audiences
stated_cause: Twitter cut off Meerkat's access to the Twitter social graph with about two hours' notice during SXSW 2015, having just acquired the competing Periscope and stating openly that competing products could not use the API. The team pivoted to Houseparty.

name: VoiceLabs
one_line: The first ad network letting Alexa skill developers earn money via sponsored messages.
audience: Third-party Alexa voice-app developers
stated_cause: Amazon updated its developer agreement to ban skills containing "any advertising for third-party products or services," eliminating the company's entire business one month after public launch.

name: Shyp
one_line: On-demand shipping — a courier collected anything you wanted to mail and packed and posted it for a flat fee.
audience: Urban consumers and small resellers who hated going to the post office
stated_cause: Imitated the Uber model but "were unable to figure out a profitable business model" — the per-pickup cost of human couriers never fit under a flat consumer fee.

name: Take Eat Easy
one_line: Courier network giving independent restaurants a delivery service.
audience: City diners and small restaurants without their own delivery
stated_cause: "Their margins were insufficient" — low ticket sizes and gross profit per order in a hyperlocal marketplace that could not leverage pre-existing supply and demand in new cities.

name: PepperTap
one_line: App to order groceries from local markets with fast delivery.
audience: Indian urban households
stated_cause: Customers found the delivery fees too expensive for their needs, and the margins on low-value grocery baskets could not carry the delivery cost.

name: Teforia
one_line: $400+ connected tea brewing machine that infused leaves to a per-varietal profile.
audience: Affluent tea enthusiasts
stated_cause: Classified as "no market need" — the market for an expensive connected single-purpose kitchen appliance never materialised at the volume required.

name: Habitual
one_line: Habit-tracking app with streaks and reminders.
audience: Self-improvement consumers building daily routines
stated_cause: Failed on marketing and distribution — the product existed in a category with hundreds of near-identical entrants and never found a channel.

name: Kopely
one_line: Stress-relief and wellness mobile app.
audience: Stressed working adults
stated_cause: "COVID-19 changed things when development partners were no longer interested in building the app" — the company depended on an outside build partner it could not replace.

name: Refolo
one_line: Plant-based meal planning app.
audience: New and aspiring plant-based eaters
stated_cause: Bad market fit — the team could not find a segment for whom plant-based meal planning was an acute enough problem to pay for.
